3.text: Thus, besides the “maiden-children,” the Russian creoles have also “widow-

4.text: children,” and the joint number in both categories forms about thirty per cent

5.text: of all the Russian infants. Exactly the same proportion exists among the

6.text: Chukchee. Some Russian families, numerous and well-to-do, have at their

7.text: head an old female who bore all her children in the maiden state. Even the

8.text: family names are derived from a Christian name of such a maiden patriarch,

9.text: or rather matriarch; for instance, Наташонки (“sons of Nathalie”), Катьконки

10.text: (“sons of Kate”), etc. There are families in which aversion to marriage has

11.text: even acquired a morbid character. The people say that in such families old

12.text: mothers will take an oath from their sons that they will never marry. “You

13.text: may live in fornication, if you desire it; but to your marriage I shall not

14.text: give my blessing.” Their aim is to extinguish their name. The daughters

15.text: are allowed to marry. The two rich families, Chertkov and Uvarovsky, are

16.text: said to have stood under such an oath in the last generation. The first family

17.text: has already vanished. The second one contains two brothers. Both have

18.text: paramours and children; but, since they are not married, their children bear

19.text: another name. All this is told on the Kolyma from mouth to mouth with

20.text: many comments, though I cannot tell how far it is true. Still, I have noticed

21.text: also among the Russianized Yukaghir of the Lower Kolyma, who are rapidly

22.text: dying out, the same morbid aversion to marriage, though in connection with

23.text: other facts. “Too much trouble,” say these wretched people in reference to

24.text: marriage.¹ The Russian creoles are dying out only a little more slowly than

26.text: Syphilis has also taken quite deep root among the Russian creoles. The

27.text: blood of new generations is tainted, and the remnant of their vigor is dying

28.text: away. Card-playing in its worst forms is also widely spread among the Russian

29.text: creoles. Games of hazard prevail; and regular cheating, even among the

30.text: upper crust, is almost considered a lawful means of winning a fortune. Social

31.text: relations are harsh and egotistic. All the people who are a little better off

32.text: than others lend money or food in small quantities at fabulous rates; two

33.text: hundred per cent yearly, and even more, being charged; and even the poorest

34.text: people consider this as quite natural. “Why,” explained one of the poorest

35.text: debtors to me, “since he had a chance, he pressed me dry. If I could, I

36.text: should do the same to him.” On the Lower Kolyma such mutual relations

37.text: assume an almost artless character. All are quite poor, all charge each other

38.text: large percentages and demand heavy payments, and in the end nobody receives

39.text: anything. The amounts are credited, and the credits balance very nearly.

40.text: Even taxes and other exactions are hardly paid by the community.
